text: What is an Operating System?

options.text: A type of hardware that controls the CPU
A program or set of programs that drives the hardware and provides an interface between the user and the computer
A network protocol for sharing files
A program used only for file management

explanation: An OS is a program, or set of programs, that drives the hardware and provides an interface between the user and the computer.

text: Why is the Operating System kept separate from other files and data on a computer?

options.text: To protect it from being corrupted or deleted, which would stop the computer working
To allow multiple users to access it
Because it is too large to store with other files

explanation: The OS is kept separate to protect it. In early computers it wasn't separated, making it vulnerable to corruption or deletion by other files or users.

text: What are the TWO main types of Operating System?
explanation: The two main types of OS are Single User and Multi User.

text: What is a Single User Operating System also known as?
explanation: Single User operating systems allow only one user at a time and are sometimes called Stand-alone Systems.

text: How does a Single Processor system give the impression of doing many things at once?

options.text: It uses multiple CPUs working in parallel
It allocates a tiny amount of processor time to each user or task in turn — called time-slicing
It stores tasks in RAM and processes them all together
It uses the GPU to handle extra tasks

explanation: Time-slicing splits processor time between tasks by allocating tiny amounts to each in turn, giving the impression of simultaneous processing.

text: Why doesn't doubling the number of CPU cores double the processing speed?

options.text: Cores share the same RAM so slow each other down
Communication between cores is needed and uses some of the extra processing speed
The OS can only use one core at a time
Extra cores increase power consumption which throttles performance

explanation: Doubling cores doesn't double speed because cores need to communicate with each other, and that overhead uses up some of the extra speed gained.

text: What are the two main types of multi-tasking strategy?
explanation: Pre-emptive multi-tasking is where the OS handles switching between tasks. Co-operative multi-tasking is where each task relinquishes control at an appropriate stage.

text: In pre-emptive multi-tasking, who is responsible for switching resources between tasks?
explanation: In pre-emptive multi-tasking the OS handles all switching of resources between tasks — the applications have no control over this.

text: In co-operative multi-tasking, how does task switching work?

options.text: The OS forces tasks to stop at set intervals
Each task relinquishes control at an appropriate stage
The CPU automatically switches between tasks
Tasks are queued and processed one at a time

explanation: In co-operative multi-tasking, each task decides when to give up control — the OS does not force it.

text: What is a Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) used for?

options.text: Direct control over electromechanical equipment, reacting to situations instantaneously
Allowing multiple users to share a single processor
Managing file storage on a network

explanation: RTOS is used for direct control over electromechanical equipment, reacting to changing situations in real time.

text: What are Batch Systems typically used for?

options.text: Running large operations overnight or as background processes
Controlling hardware devices in real time
Providing a GUI for end users

explanation: Batch Systems run large batch operations, often overnight or as background processes where immediate interaction isn't needed.

text: How many layers does a modern layered Operating System have?
explanation: A layered OS has 5 layers: Kernel, Memory Management, Input/Output, File Management System, and User Interface.

text: Starting from the most protected, what is the correct order of the 5 OS layers?

options.text: User Interface → File Management → I/O → Memory Management → Kernel
Kernel → Memory Management → Input/Output → File Management → User Interface
Kernel → User Interface → File Management → I/O → Memory Management
Memory Management → Kernel → I/O → File Management → User Interface

explanation: From most protected to least: Kernel → Memory Management → Input/Output → File Management System → User Interface.

text: Which layer of the OS has the GREATEST level of protection?
explanation: The Kernel has the greatest level of protection as it is the core of the OS. The User Interface has the least.

text: Which layer of the OS has the LEAST level of protection?
explanation: The User Interface has the least protection — it is the outermost layer that users interact with directly.

text: What is the role of the User Interface layer in the OS?

options.text: To manage how files are stored on disk
To allow the user to interact directly with the operating system
To control input and output devices at a hardware level
To protect the Kernel from corruption

explanation: The User Interface layer allows the user to interact directly with the OS — loading programs, modifying settings and requesting information.

text: What is the role of the File Management layer of the OS?

options.text: To provide the graphical interface for the user
To organise and manage the storage of data on permanent media
To handle communication between CPU cores
To manage how RAM is allocated to running programs

explanation: The File Management layer is responsible for organising and managing storage of data on permanent media such as hard drives and removable storage.

text: What does the Memory Management layer of the OS do?

options.text: Manages how files are saved to disk
Handles the graphical display of windows and icons
Controls how RAM is allocated and managed between running programs
Controls the boot sequence when the computer starts

explanation: The Memory Management layer controls how RAM is allocated and managed between running programs, ensuring each gets the memory it needs without interfering with others.

text: Which OS layer sits directly above the Kernel?
explanation: The layer order from most to least protected is: Kernel → Memory Management → Input/Output → File Management → User Interface. Memory Management sits directly above the Kernel.

text: Which OS layer sits directly below the User Interface?
explanation: The order from most to least protected is: Kernel → Memory Management → I/O → File Management → User Interface. File Management sits directly below the User Interface.

text: What does CLI stand for?
explanation: CLI stands for Command Line Interface — where the user types commands at a prompt on screen, such as the C:> prompt in MS-DOS.

text: Which operating systems still use CLI heavily?
explanation: UNIX and Linux still use CLI heavily. Windows has a CLI available via Command Prompt but is primarily GUI-based.

text: What is a 'switch' in a CLI command?

options.text: A network device used to connect computers
A modifier added to a command to change how it executes or displays output
A key pressed to switch between open programs
A way to switch between CLI and GUI mode

explanation: A switch modifies how a command executes or displays output. For example 'dir windows /p' lists files but pauses when the screen is full.

text: What does WIMP stand for in relation to GUI interfaces?
explanation: WIMP stands for Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointers — the key elements of a Graphical User Interface.

text: What is the primary hard drive typically assigned as in Windows?
explanation: C: is the primary hard drive in Windows. A: and B: were traditionally floppy drives. D: is typically the DVD drive.

text: What is the Master Boot Record (MBR)?

options.text: A file that stores user passwords
The first sectors of a drive containing boot instructions and partition table information
A table that tracks file locations on a FAT volume
A backup copy of the OS stored in ROM

explanation: The MBR is in the first sectors of the drive. The BIOS loads and runs it to start the OS. It holds partition table information for up to 4 primary partitions.

text: What is the boot sequence?

options.text: The order of layers in the OS
The order in which the computer searches drives for an OS to boot from
The startup checklist run by the file management layer
The sequence of steps to defragment a drive

explanation: The boot sequence is the order in which the BIOS searches drives for an OS to boot from. It can be changed in BIOS settings.

text: What are the circular storage bands on a hard disk platter called?
explanation: Each platter is divided into thin concentric bands called tracks. Tracks are further subdivided into sectors, each 512 bytes in size.

text: What is the standard size of a sector on a traditional hard disk?
explanation: Sectors are 512 bytes on traditional hard disks. Newer drives use 4KB sectors to allow larger TB-scale capacities.

text: What is a cylinder on a hard disk?

options.text: A single track on one platter
A group of tracks with the same track number across different platters
The spindle that the platters are mounted on
A cluster of sectors on a single platter

explanation: A cylinder is a group of tracks that share the same track number but are on different platters — essentially a vertical column through the disk stack.

text: What are clusters in the context of file storage?

options.text: Groups of servers connected in a network
Groups of sectors combined into larger units that the file system uses to store files
The read/write heads on a hard disk platter
Backup copies of the file allocation table

explanation: The File Management Layer groups sectors into clusters. Files are stored in units of clusters rather than individual sectors.

text: Why is disk defragmentation needed?

options.text: To remove viruses from the hard disk
Because deleting and writing files scatters fragments across the disk, slowing read/write speeds
To increase the size of sectors on the disk
To reformat the disk and remove old file systems

explanation: When files are deleted and new ones written, fragments get scattered. The read heads must seek out non-contiguous clusters, slowing performance. Defragmentation reorganises them.

text: What does FAT stand for?
explanation: FAT stands for File Allocation Table. Versions include FAT12, FAT16 and FAT32.

text: What are the four file attributes that can be set on a FAT file?
explanation: A FAT file has four attribute bits: Archive, System, Hidden and Read-only.

text: What minimum drive size does FAT32 support compared to earlier FAT versions?
explanation: FAT32 supports drives with over 2GB of storage, which earlier FAT versions could not handle.

text: What is the key advantage of NTFS over FAT32?

options.text: FAT32 supports larger files than NTFS
NTFS is more secure and reliable, supporting encryption, compression and access control
NTFS is an older, simpler system
FAT32 uses a Master File Table while NTFS uses a File Allocation Table

explanation: NTFS is more secure and reliable than FAT. It supports data access control, ownership privileges, file compression and encryption.

text: What does NTFS use to track files on a volume?
explanation: NTFS uses a Master File Table (MFT) which holds records of all files on the volume. NTFS file access is very fast compared to FAT.

text: What is file locking and why is it needed?

options.text: Encrypting a file so only the owner can read it
Preventing two users from amending the same file simultaneously, which could cause data corruption
Setting a file as read-only permanently
Compressing a file to save disk space

explanation: In a multi-user system two users might try to access the same file simultaneously. File locking prevents simultaneous amendments that could corrupt data. A second user can still open a read-only copy.

text: What is record locking?

options.text: Locking an entire file so no one else can open it
Splitting a large file into sections so only parts of it are locked at a time
Storing records in encrypted format on disk
A method of defragmenting database files

explanation: Record locking splits large files into sections so only the part in use is locked, keeping the rest available to other users.

text: Which company created Network File System (NFS) and in what year?
explanation: Sun Microsystems created NFS in 1985, making it the first widely used network file system.
